findings.title: Pin and verify the remote install script or drop the curl|sh line
findings.whyItBreaks: The image build now executes `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` as root with no version/commit pin, no checksum, and no signature verification. example.com is a reserved documentation domain (RFC 2606), not a real distribution endpoint, so this is either a placeholder that would ship as-is or a dangling URL outside the repo's control; whoever controls the host (or a redirect target, since -L follows redirects) can change the script and inject arbitrary code into every image build and every CI run that runs this Dockerfile. The local `RUN apk add curl` and the COPY/CMD instructions do not mitigate this: the added line is the only new capability and it is entirely unverified remote execution.

findings.title: Fail the build on download error instead of running an empty script
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL` omits `-f`, so HTTP 4xx/5xx does not make curl exit non-zero, and `-s` hides the error. A failed download pipes empty stdin into `sh`, which exits 0, so the RUN layer and the whole build succeed while the intended install never happened (TRIGGER D: the download error signal is discarded and mapped to success). If the purpose of this layer is to provide software the image depends on, the image silently ships without it and the failure is indistinguishable from a working install to every later stage and consumer.

findings.title: Do not curl|sh unpinned remote script during image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The added RUN executes a script downloaded from an HTTPS URL at image build time, piped directly into `sh` running as root inside the build container. There is no version pin, no checksum/hash verification, and no attestation of the artifact; the resulting behavior of `/app` is silently coupled to whatever the third-party host serves when the image is built, and the injected content is baked into the produced image. `-sL` also follows arbitrary redirects without notice. Because the URL is `example.com` (RFC 2606 reserved placeholder — not a real install endpoint), the fetched body is an HTML page rather than a valid install script, so `sh` will fail to interpret it and the `RUN` step exits non-zero, aborting `docker build` and leaving the image unusable. Navigation/audit-trail behavior of the application itself is unaffected, but the build path is broken and any substitute real URL reintroduces the unpinned remote-code-execution surface.

findings.title: Pin and verify the remote install script instead of piping curl to sh
findings.whyItBreaks: RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh pipes arbitrary remote content directly into sh on every image build with no checksum, GPG signature, version, or commit pin. If the URL host is compromised or the upstream payload changes, the rebuilt image silently gains attacker-controlled code with no diffusion through review. The URL is also the RFC 2606 placeholder domain example.com, so today the fetched payload is unverifiable/unofficial. This is a supply-chain defect on the build surface.

findings.title: Make install-step fetch failure abort the build
findings.whyItBreaks: curl -s suppresses progress and error messages but lacks -f, so an HTTP 404 or network failure yields empty (or partial) stdout instead of a hard error. The pipeline's exit status is sh's, and sh reading empty stdin exits 0, so RUN 'succeeds' on a failed download. The image is then built and deployed, silently missing the tooling this step was meant to install; no consumer can distinguish the failed install from a successful one.

findings.title: Propagate the error in LoadOrDefault instead of discarding it
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault is exported and discards Load's error return with `v, _ := Load(key, m)` (store.go:16). On a missing key, Load returns ("", ErrMissing) (store.go:10), so LoadOrDefault returns "" — a caller cannot distinguish 'key absent' from 'key present with an empty value'. A misconfigured/typo'd key silently yields the zero value instead of surfacing ErrMissing, and any error type Load may return in the future is also flattened to "". Because the function is public, this conflation is the contract for every future caller; the fallback is implicit (zero value), not an explicit, agreed-upon default.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing; missing key is indistinguishable from empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing when the key is absent (store.go:10) but returns ("", nil) for a key present with an empty value (store.go:12). LoadOrDefault discards the error with `v, _ :=` (store.go:16) and returns "" in both cases, so no caller can distinguish 'lookup failed' from a legitimate empty-string value — the failure value equals a real value. The default is not caller-customizable, nothing logs the dropped ErrMissing, and the function is exported, so every future caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value (TRIGGER D, exported-swallow rule applies even with no in-repo callers).

findings.title: Join goroutines before Run returns; close-after-Run panics and writes are lost
findings.whyItBreaks: Base wrote results <- j*2 synchronously for every job, so when Run returned all writes had completed; callers could then close `results` or stop draining safely. Head spawns an unjoined goroutine per job and returns immediately: in-flight sends race the caller - closing the channel now panics (send on closed channel), and a caller that drains then proceeds loses writes (buffered channel: pending sends sit undrained forever; unbuffered: every goroutine blocks until a reader arrives, with nondeterministic ordering). The function's public contract silently changed from synchronous producer to fire-and-forget with no completion signal.

findings.title: Honor ctx in spawned goroutines; blocking sends leak on cancellation
findings.whyItBreaks: Each goroutine blocks on `results <- j * 2` until a reader arrives, and none select on ctx.Done. If the caller cancels ctx and stops draining (a pattern the passed-in ctx parameter exists to support), every pending goroutine blocks forever - a goroutine leak that never existed before, because base's synchronous sends could not outlive Run.

findings.title: Return completes before results are sent; races with close and leaks goroutines
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code sent each result synchronously, so 'Run returned' implied all len(jobs) values had been delivered to results (chan<- owned by the caller) in job order. Head code spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately, before any send necessarily completes. Consequences: (1) the canonical caller pattern of closing the producer channel once Run returns now races with in-flight sends -> 'send on closed channel' process panic; (2) a barrier-style caller that awaits Run and then returns without draining all len(jobs) values leaves the send goroutines blocked forever on the unbuffered channel (goroutine leak, and ctx cancellation cannot unblock them); (3) delivered values are now in nondeterministic order, so a caller that positionally maps the i-th received value to jobs[i] silently gets wrong associations. The single-line body change silently drops the function's completion/ordering contract while the unchanged public signature keeps promising a plain synchronous Run.

findings.title: Make Run wait for spawned goroutines before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior: `results <- j * 2` executed synchronously inside Run, so returning from Run guaranteed all len(jobs) results were delivered to the channel. Head behavior: the send runs in a fire-and-forget goroutine, so Run returns as soon as goroutines are scheduled, before any send happens-before the return (Go memory model gives no synchronization edge). A caller that, per the previous contract, closes `results` right after Run returns now races with pending sends and panics with 'send on closed channel', and a caller that reads after Run returns may observe fewer than len(jobs) results or time out while goroutines were never scheduled. No WaitGroup/done-channel/ctx-cancellation mechanism exists to re-establish the completion signal.

findings.title: Implement or remove the ignored `tag` parameter in Log()
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature `Log(message string, tag ...string)` (src/logger.go:3) is a contract carrier: the parameter name `tag` promises the supplied tags are emitted with the message. The body (src/logger.go:4) is still only `println(message)` and never reads `tag`, so every caller who passes a tag — e.g. `Log("started", "worker-7")` — will search the logs by that tag and find nothing, because the tag is silently dropped. This is contract drift introduced by the diff: the type change newly promises a behavior that the unchanged body does not implement, and the unmet promise changes exactly the emitted data a caller receives (the log line). It is a present defect in the public API contract even though no in-repo caller uses the new parameter yet.

findings.title: Restore AND in canDeleteRecord: OR bypasses tenant isolation and ownership
findings.whyItBreaks: The change from && to || weakens the delete gate in two independent ways. Before: a record could be deleted only by an admin of the SAME tenant as the record (isAdmin && tenantId equal). After: (a) any admin can delete records in ANY tenant (tenantId check is bypassed whenever isAdmin is true), enabling cross-tenant deletion / tenant-isolation bypass; (b) any non-admin user whose tenantId matches the record can delete it, with no requirement that the session owns the record (RecordRef.ownerId exists but is never consulted) and no admin requirement. This is a direct privilege escalation in an exported authorization predicate whose semantics are the security contract; a malicious admin in tenant A can delete tenant B's records, and any authenticated tenant member can delete unowned records.

findings.title: Restore tenant+admin gate: OR grants cross-tenant delete to any admin
findings.whyItBreaks: The change replaces `isAdmin && tenantId===record.tenantId` with `isAdmin || tenantId===record.tenantId`, widening the delete authorization predicate in two independent ways: (a) the admin branch loses its tenant scope, so an admin of tenant A can now delete records in every other tenant; (b) the tenant-match branch loses the admin requirement, so any non-admin session whose tenant matches can delete the record regardless of who owns it (RecordRef.ownerId / Session.userId are never consulted). Both request shapes returned false at base (verified via git show 5526408:src/permissions.ts) and now return true, and TRIGGER A (over-block) does not apply — this is the inverse, an under-block/privilege escalation on a public authorization gate.

findings.title: Revert canDeleteRecord to &&; || allows non-admin and cross-tenant deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: The base predicate required BOTH isAdmin AND tenant equality (tenant-scoped admin-only delete). Substituting concrete values into the new `||` predicate: (1) Session{isAdmin:false, tenantId:'A'} over Record{tenantId:'A'} — base=false (denied), head=true: any same-tenant non-admin can now delete records, a privilege escalation since delete was admin-only; (2) Session{isAdmin:true, tenantId:'A'} over Record{tenantId:'B'} — base=false (denied), head=true: any admin from any tenant can now delete records in other tenants, breaking the tenant isolation the base code deliberately enforced. This ships a less restrictive security gate to every external caller of this exported predicate; the deleted data is unrecoverable.

findings.title: Preserve valid fields instead of returning full defaults on any parse error
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch treats EVERY failure identically: a JSON parse error OR a single field validation failure (throws at lines 11-12, now dead code swallowed by the catch) all produce a fresh { ...DEFAULTS }. So a partially-valid doc like raw = '{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"17"}' returns {theme:"light",fontSize:14}, discarding the user's valid theme along with the bad fontSize field. The live write path updateFontSize (line 19-23) then calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)) at line 22 and persists {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>} over the user's real settings — silently resetting a valid preference to default. Old behavior threw 'bad fontSize' and never reached save. Additionally, parseSettings is exported/public, so any caller can no longer distinguish corrupt config from legitimately-default config (TRIGGER D: failure mapped to an honest-looking default value).

findings.title: Do not swallow settings parse errors into defaults before a save
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch-all maps every failure (bad JSON plus the two explicit 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' validation throws at lines 11-12) to { ...DEFAULTS }. In the only in-repo caller, updateFontSize(raw, size, save) at lines 19-22, a corrupt/partially-written persisted raw string now returns defaults, has fontSize overwritten, and is written back via save(JSON.stringify(...)). Before this change the error propagated and save() was never reached, so stored settings (including any valid portion, e.g. theme, if only fontSize was corrupt) were preserved and the failure was surfaced. Now the failure is indistinguishable from a legitimate default and the fallback is persisted, silently overwriting stored settings on a live mutation path. Severity held at P2: the trigger requires already-corrupt stored settings (exceptional state), so this is a data-loss regression but not a main-path blocking defect.

findings.title: Restore error propagation in parseSettings instead of returning DEFAULTS on any failure
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously malformed JSON, non-string theme, or non-number fontSize threw, so callers could catch and react (show an error, keep last-known-good settings, skip persisting). Now every one of those signals is swallowed and replaced with { theme: 'light', fontSize: 14 }, and because parsing does not fail, consumers cannot distinguish corrupt input from a legitimate value. Any read-then-persist caller (e.g. updateFontSize, which saves JSON.stringify of the parse result) will silently overwrite the user's stored settings with defaults on transient or corrupt input, losing their real preferences without any error surface. parseSettings is an exported/public API with no doc comment promising this fallback, and nothing logs the failure, so this is a present contract defect shipping now even with no in-repo callers yet.

findings.title: Report artifacts from 'verified' ref while builtFrom still claims branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The change fetches a second ref (verified) and passes it to artifactsAt, while builtFrom is still the branch ref (commit). The exported BuildReport field name 'builtFrom' promises the commit the listed artifacts were built from; when ref('verified') differs from ref(branch) — the only reason this change has any effect — the report attributes artifacts to a commit they did not come from, and the actual source (verified) is reported nowhere. Previously both fields were guaranteed consistent; this PR breaks that invariant. A caller rendering or diffing against builtFrom will use the wrong commit.

findings.title: Report artifacts from 'verified' ref while builtFrom claims the branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported buildReport(build, branch) contract pairs a commit with the artifacts built from it. The diff adds verified = build.ref("verified") and returns { builtFrom: commit, artifacts: build.artifactsAt(verified) }. The two fields now resolve independently: whenever ref("verified") != ref(branch) — the normal case, since a 'verified' ref typically lags or diverges from the branch tip — the report tells every caller the artifacts were built from `commit` when they actually came from another commit, and the `branch` argument no longer selects the artifacts at all. Any consumer that archives, publishes, or diffs the artifacts against builtFrom (or verifies signatures against the claimed commit) acts on the wrong pairing. This is a body-vs-carrier drift on a public signature with no in-repo mitigation: if the intent was 'report verified artifacts', builtFrom must be verified too; if the intent was branch artifacts, artifactsAt must take commit. Either way one field is wrong whenever the refs differ.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from same ref as builtFrom or both use verified
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport promises (via the exported BuildReport.builtFrom field) that builtFrom identifies the commit the returned artifacts were built from. Before this change builtFrom and artifacts both came from build.ref(branch). Now artifacts come from build.ref("verified") — a different ref — while builtFrom still records the branch ref. Any consumer of this exported function receives a report in which builtFrom and artifacts can reference two different commits, so the artifact list no longer corresponds to the commit the report claims it was built from. This is a TRIGGER C contract drift: the promised pairing (builtFrom = artifact source) is not implemented by the body at report.ts:14. Additionally, "verified" is a new hard-coded ref name that has no presence elsewhere in the repo and is not documented, so its resolution (missing-ref behavior) is unverifiable here.

findings.title: Restore slice(0, limit) in recentEntries; limit is now ignored for limit > 0
findings.whyItBreaks: This diff replaces `return [...all].reverse().slice(0, limit);` with a branch that returns the entire reversed array whenever limit > 0. The `slice(0, limit)` capping was removed, so `recentEntries(all, 5)` returns every element instead of at most 5. This violates the function's own doc contract ('Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first.', src/feed.ts:1) and breaks the only caller `renderFeed` (src/feed.ts:8-13): it allocates `new Array<string>(20)` and fills by `for (let i = 0; i < page.length; i++) out[i] = page[i]`, so when `all` has more than 20 entries (the normal feed case), `page.length` exceeds 20 and the loop writes past the intended page, returning an un-paged feed of all entries. The `limit <= 0` guard is correct (it matches original slice(0, negative)=[] behavior), but the positive-limit path is now unbounded.

findings.title: Restore slice(0, limit) removed in recentEntries limit truncation
findings.whyItBreaks: Base returned `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`; head returns the whole `sorted` array for any `limit > 0`. The doc comment still promises 'Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first', but recentEntries(all, 3) now returns every entry. renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) calls recentEntries(all, 20) relying on a page of ≤20, then copies `page.length` (now unbounded) items into `out`, so the feed renders all entries instead of a capped recent page.

findings.title: Restore the limit cap: recentEntries now returns the full list, ignoring limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code was `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`; the head version replaces it with `const sorted = [...all].reverse(); if (limit <= 0) return []; return sorted;`, silently dropping `.slice(0, limit)`. The doc comment (src/feed.ts:1) still promises 'at most `limit` entries', but for any limit > 0 the function returns all `all.length` entries. The in-repo caller renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) relies on the cap: it allocates a 20-slot array and copies page.length entries into it, so a feed with >20 items now returns every item instead of the newest 20 (the array grows past 20 via the loop at src/feed.ts:11). This is a TRIGGER C contract drift with a relying caller, plus a straight functional regression on the changed lines.

findings.title: Make entry-count reflect filtered live rows, not all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The new filter excludes stale entries from the emitted rows, but line 22 still passes `entries.length` (the pre-filter count) to headerLines. Whenever any entry has stale=true, the `# entry-count` header overstates the actual number of rows in the manifest (e.g. 2 entries, 1 stale -> header says 2, output has 1 row). Before this diff the count always equaled the row count. renderManifest is exported, so any consumer that parses entry-count to size, validate, or iterate the manifest now gets an inconsistent contract.

findings.title: Use live.length for entry-count header after stale filtering
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest filters stale entries into `live` (line 20) but still passes entries.length to headerLines (line 22). Reopened hunk confirms: `const live = entries.filter((e) => !e.stale)` maps rows from live, while the header still reads `[...headerLines(opts, entries.length), ...rows]`. Substitution: entries=[{path:'a',size:1,stale:true},{path:'b',size:2,stale:false}] renders '# entry-count: 2' followed by exactly one row. Base version (git show 75650d9:src/manifest.ts) mapped all entries to rows, so count==rows was an invariant; the diff breaks it. The '# entry-count' header is part of the exported manifest format — 'stale' is a real field on the Entry interface, so any manifest containing a stale entry emits an internally inconsistent count, and a consumer that sizes by or validates the count against rows gets a wrong result or parse error. If stale entries were meant to remain listed, the filter itself is wrong; either way the output is inconsistent. Bug is fully observable within this single changed file. SuggestedFix resolves it.

score.error: opencode runner exited 1; stderr withheld because it may contain the review prompt

findings.title: execute() now always throws, breaking its string-return contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `return input.toUpperCase()` with an unconditional `throw new Error("always fails")`. The exported signature `execute(input: string): string` (src/runner.ts:1) promises a returned string, but no code path returns anymore — every invocation raises an exception. Any consumer of this module receives a crash instead of a value; the function's entire purpose is disabled. The change is a pure regression with no feature/flag justification in the diff.

findings.title: Restore execute() to return the transformed string instead of always throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: This is the module's sole exported function and its only code path. Base commit 91bf681 returned input.toUpperCase(); head unconditionally throws Error('always fails') for every input, so any consumer calling execute() gets an unhandled exception instead of the promised string. The exported API is rendered completely unusable regardless of input, a direct regression of working behavior.

findings.title: Restore execute() to return a value instead of throwing unconditionally
findings.whyItBreaks: execute() is the sole exported function of this module; its signature `(input: string): string` (src/runner.ts:1) contracts a string result, and the base version computed it via toUpperCase(). The change replaces that with an unconditional `throw new Error("always fails")`, so every caller now receives an exception instead of a value — the function is unusable in all cases, `input` is dead, and any consumer (library import or downstream service) crashes on the happy path. TRIGGER C fires: public carrier `execute(input: string): string` @src/runner.ts:1 promises a string result, body @src/runner.ts:2 always throws; the promise-vs-body mismatch affects exactly the data a caller receives (they get a crash, never a result), and for an exported symbol the promise itself is the contract even with no in-repo caller (verified: rg finds no callers of execute/runner anywhere in the repo).

findings.title: Remove viewer rejection or update handle: active viewers now get 'rejected', not 'read-only'
findings.whyItBreaks: handle() (src/handler.ts:23-28) still contains `if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only";` (line 25), which is its own stated contract that an eligible viewer is served read-only access. The new guard `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` makes isEligible reject exactly that value: for a viewer with status 'active' and attempts < 5, base behavior was isEligible=true -> handle() -> 'read-only'; head behavior is isEligible=false -> 'rejected'. The same file thus rejects an action (read-only serving) that it deems legitimately approvable one line later, and line 25 becomes unreachable. Either the viewer-rejection is wrong (viewers lose a legitimate outcome), or the rejection was intended and the 'read-only' branch should have been removed — the diff leaves the public handle() contract contradicting itself.

findings.title: Remove viewer rejection in isEligible; it dead-codes the read-only path in handle
findings.whyItBreaks: The added guard `if (req.role === "viewer") return false` in isEligible makes handle() return "rejected" for every viewer, even an active viewer with attempts < 5. handle() itself still defines the viewer outcome as legitimate (`if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only";` at src/handler.ts:25), so that branch is now unreachable dead code — direct evidence the eligibility change was not intended to eliminate the viewer outcome. Base behavior for {status:"active", role:"viewer", attempts:0} was "read-only"; head returns "rejected". isEligible is also exported, so the rejection leaks into every external caller's eligibility decision.

findings.title: Drop viewer gate in isEligible or remove now-dead read-only branch in handle
findings.whyItBreaks: The added `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` makes isEligible reject viewers before handle() ever dispatches, so a viewer request that previously reached the retained `if (req.role === "viewer") return "read-only";` branch (line 25) now returns "rejected" at line 24. The read-only branch is unreachable dead code after this change, yet it was deliberately kept — evidence that viewers were meant to be served read-only. The eligibility gate's prior concern (status/attempts retry budget) did not cover role; injecting the role check silently changes an externally observable outcome (viewer response string) and contradicts the existing role dispatch, so the guard rejects an action that was legitimately approvable on its own.

findings.title: Do not gate saveDraft on payment status
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed gates two distinct actions. For submitOrder the new payment check is legitimate, but saveDraft is the action that exists precisely for incomplete (unpaid) orders. With the changed predicate, an order in state "draft" with payment "missing" — previously allowed — is now rejected by canProceed, so saveDraft returns "blocked" and a user can no longer save an unpaid draft. The predicate over-blocks a draft save that is independently approvable (state is still draft, nothing is being submitted).

findings.title: Restrict payment check to submit; saveDraft now rejects unpaid drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is shared by two distinct actions. submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) legitimately requires payment, but saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9) does not — a draft with payment="missing" is an explicitly legal state (Order.payment: "missing" | "paid", src/policy.ts:3) and saving it is approvable on its own. After this change, saveDraft returns "blocked" for any unpaid draft, so users can no longer persist drafts before payment (precondition substitution: payment="missing" → guard order.payment === "paid" @src/policy.ts:7 → false → "blocked" @src/actions.ts:9). Previously only the state check applied, so this is a regression in the save path.

findings.title: Move payment check to submitOrder; it wrongly blocks draft saving
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed now requires payment === 'paid', but it is also the gate for saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). An order with state 'draft' and payment 'missing' previously saved ('saved'), and is legitimately approvable on its own — saving a draft is independent of payment. The changed predicate now rejects it ('blocked'), a P2 regression on the save-draft action. The payment gate is only legitimate for the submit action (src/actions.ts:4).

findings.title: Return filesAt(head) so snapshot files match the snapshot commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The snapshot's commit field is the channel head (commit: head, line 16) but files are now repo.filesAt(stable) (line 18), where stable = repo.headCommit("stable") (line 14). For any channel != "stable", the returned Snapshot pairs commit X with the file list of a different commit Y, so the snapshot's files do not correspond to its commit. Base behavior (git show 2b0b13f:src/publish.ts) returned files: repo.filesAt(head), keeping commit and files consistent. Any consumer that checks out/uses the snapshot commit and expects the listed files (integrity check, publishing the files under the commit label, diffing) acts on wrong data for every non-stable channel.

findings.title: Return files for the snapshot's own commit, not a hardcoded 'stable' ref
findings.whyItBreaks: The returned Snapshot now claims commit=headCommit(channel) and channel=<channel> but sets files=filesAt(headCommit("stable")). For every channel other than "stable" — including DEFAULT_CHANNEL "main" — the file list describes a different ref than the snapshot's commit, so any consumer that deploys, diffs, or lists the files for snapshot.commit publishes/verifies the wrong file set under the wrong commit tag. Additionally, the previously working call path (base behavior: files=filesAt(headCommit(channel))) now unconditionally dereferences an undeclared ref: nothing in the repo creates or documents a "stable" ref, so a previously valid publish for any channel either fails if headCommit throws on a missing ref or returns an empty/garbage file list if it returns null. This is a regression of the function's existing contract: snapshot.files no longer corresponds to snapshot.commit.

findings.title: Restore commit/files consistency in publishSnapshot; drop hardcoded 'stable'
findings.whyItBreaks: Base returned files: repo.filesAt(head) with head = headCommit(channel), so files always described the reported commit. Head keeps commit: headCommit(channel) but computes files: repo.filesAt(headCommit("stable")) (src/publish.ts:14,18). The exported Snapshot contract (commit + files of one state) now promises a state it does not hold: any consumer that reads blob contents, diffs, or dedupes using snapshot.commit against snapshot.files gets files from a different ref. Additionally the hardcoded "stable" ref changes behavior for every channel: repos without a stable ref make headCommit (typed to return string, so likely throwing) fail publishSnapshot for ALL channels, whereas base worked for any existing channel; and for a channel other than "stable", the snapshot silently publishes the wrong files under the wrong commit label. If publishing stable's state was intended, commit/channel must be set to the stable head consistently; otherwise files should come from head.

findings.title: Use the new `limit` parameter instead of hardcoded max_count
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff adds public parameter `build(prefix, limit=10)` but the body still computes `range(max_count)` with `max_count = 10` hardcoded at line 2; `limit` never flows into the loop. The parameter name promises a cap on the returned list, and the promise affects the result a caller receives: `build('x', limit=3)` returns 10 items and `build('x', limit=100)` also returns 10. Since `build` is a public module-level function, the promise itself is the contract (capping is the explicitly listed promised behavior), so this is a P2 even with no in-repo caller yet. Default behavior is unchanged (limit=10 == max_count=10), only non-default calls are wrong.

findings.title: Honor the new `limit` parameter in build()'s loop
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff adds `limit=10` to the public signature of `build()`, but the body still hardcodes `max_count = 10` (src/builder.py:2) and iterates `range(max_count)` (line 4); `limit` is never read. Any caller that passes `limit=3` or `limit=100` silently receives exactly 10 items — the parameter promises output capping that the body does not implement. This is a public (non-underscore) module-level function, so the parameter name itself is the contract: a caller relying on the promise (e.g., batch sizing) gets a wrong result with no error. Default behavior is unchanged only because the default (10) coincides with the hardcoded count.

findings.title: parse_positive_int name promises positivity but body never validates
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff renames the public module-level function read_int to parse_positive_int in a validators.py module, changing the contract carrier to promise 'positive' validation, but the body is unchanged: return int(value) accepts zero and negatives. TRIGGER C: promise (validates/rejects non-positive input) != body (plain int conversion, no check). Any caller that trusts the new name and skips its own positivity check will receive 0 or a negative amount instead of an error — e.g. charge(-5) silently returns -500, total_cents(-5) returns -500. This is an exported carrier (module-level, no underscore, no __all__ restriction), so the promise itself is the contract and the defect ships now even though no in-repo caller exists yet; the promised behavior directly affects the value a caller receives.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy to avoid mutating caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `df.copy()` was the function's non-mutation contract: previously apply_values returned a new frame and left the input untouched; now it writes `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` into the caller's own DataFrame and returns the same object (`out is df` is True). Any caller that reuses `df` after the call (comparing original vs transformed values, processing the same frame again, or passing a shared/sliced frame) now silently sees overwritten data. If a caller passes a view/slice of a parent frame, the .loc assignment also triggers pandas SettingWithCopyWarning and the write may not propagate to the parent frame. The copy was the only thing making the function side-effect-free, and its removal is not reflected in any signature or doc change.

findings.title: Restore df.copy(); apply_values now mutates the caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version deliberately returned a copy: `result = df.copy()` then writes on `result`, leaving the input untouched. The diff removes the copy and writes `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` directly on the caller's frame. Any caller that keeps using `df` after the call (re-applying a different mapping, persisting/rendering the original rows, comparing pre/post values) now observes silently overwritten data, and a second call with a different mapping only partially overwrites rows left by the first — a data-corruption regression of the public helper's previous copy semantics. This is the explicitly in-scope 'dropped defensive copy / in-place mutation of caller data' defect class.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy in apply_values to stop mutating caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Base version returned a copy (result = df.copy()) so the caller's frame was untouched; the change now writes df.loc[...] directly and returns df. Any caller that holds onto the original frame — for a second transform, reporting, comparison, or persistence — silently sees the overwritten values after this call. Dropped defensive copy / in-place mutation of caller data is a real defect class, and this is a contract regression introduced solely by this PR.

findings.title: Rename parse_positive_int promises positivity the body does not enforce
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER C: the public symbol 'parse_positive_int' is a contract carrier that promises 'positive' — a caller passing "-5" legitimately expects rejection/zeroing and instead receives -5, which then flows through charge() as -500. The body at src/parse.rs:2 is unchanged from read_int: s.parse().unwrap_or(0) — it parses any i64 including negatives and returns it as-is, and on parse failure returns 0 (which is itself not positive). The promise (positivity filter) affects the result a caller receives, and this is an exported pub fn, so the promise is the contract even with no in-repo caller relying on it yet. The rename also breaks source compatibility for any existing external consumer of read_int.

findings.title: Rename promise to parse_positive_int but body performs no validation
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER C fires: the public symbol name is a contract carrier that promises 'positive' (validated, non-negative result), but the body is unchanged `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` (src/parse.rs:2, verified against base c315f66). No positivity check exists: parse_positive_int("-5") returns -5 and parse_positive_int("abc") returns 0. The name re-presents the old failure-to-zero swallow as a validated positive parser, so callers who trust the name (e.g. charge at src/parse.rs:6-7, which feeds this value into n * 100) will compute -500 for "-5" and 0 for garbage amounts with no indication that validation never ran. For an exported carrier the promise itself is the contract; the promised validation affects the exact result callers receive, so this is a P2 even with no other in-repo callers (rg finds none).

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positivity but returns negatives and 0
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public function's name promises 'positive', but the unchanged body `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` performs no positivity validation: "-10".parse() returns -10 and unparseable input is mapped to 0. The only caller, charge (src/parse.rs:6), multiplies the result by 100 and returns it as a money amount, so a caller trusting the contract receives negative cents for negative input and 0 for garbage — exactly the capping/validation the name promises but the body does not implement. Per the rename rule, an exported carrier whose signature promises validation the body lacks is a defect even with no in-repo caller relying on it; here charge does rely on the value.

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves the Vec; remove it or borrow so the function compiles
findings.whyItBreaks: dbg!(items) expands to `match items { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`, which moves the non-Copy Vec<String> out of `items`. Line 3 then reads items.len() on a moved value, a compile error (E0382: use of moved value) — the whole crate fails to build, and the new line also dumps the full Vec to stderr on every call of this public function. The base version compiled fine; this one line breaks it.

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves `items`; following items.len() fails to compile
findings.whyItBreaks: The dbg! macro expands to `match items { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`; the match arm binds `tmp` by value (move) because the scrutinee is a non-Copy place and no match ergonomics apply, and since the statement discards the macro's returned value, `items` is dropped at line 2. Line 3 `let total = items.len();` then reads a moved value and the crate fails to build with E0382 "borrow of moved value: `items`". The entire crate is uncompilable until this is fixed, so every caller of process() is broken.

findings.title: Remove dbg!(items): it moves items, so src/store.rs no longer compiles
findings.whyItBreaks: std::dbg! expands to `match $val { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`, which takes `items` by value. Used as an expression statement, the returned value is dropped at the end of line 2, so `items.len()` on line 3 reads a moved value: error[E0382] use of moved value: `items`. The crate (the repo's only source file) fails to compile, making the core path unusable. Independent of the compile error, `dbg!` is a debug leftover in a `pub fn`: even if written `dbg!(&items)`, every call would print the full vector to stderr (data exposure on a public API, per-call stderr/perf cost).

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against `from`, not `latest`, to keep fromRevision consistent
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc on Changeset.fromRevision (src/changeset.ts:6-8) promises "Revision the changed paths were computed against. Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision." The diff resolves a second revision `latest = store.resolve("latest")` and computes changedPaths from it (line 18) while fromRevision still reports `from` (line 17). Substituting real values: pinnedTag is an arbitrary release tag (the entire reason it is a parameter rather than a hardcoded "latest"), so when pinnedTag != latest — the expected case for a pinning API — changedPaths covers only latest..HEAD while fromRevision advertises the pinned revision. A consumer that replays the changeset on fromRevision, as the interface contract instructs, applies a path set that does not correspond to that base: paths changed between the pinned tag and latest are silently dropped from the changeset, and paths in latest..HEAD are included even though they were never part of the pinned baseline. The exported buildChangeset signature and the unchanged interface doc make this consistency the public contract, so the defect is present even with no in-repo caller.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths from `from`, not `latest`, so it matches fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset contract (src/changeset.ts:7-8) promises fromRevision is "the revision the changed paths were computed against" and that "consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision." The diff adds `latest = store.resolve("latest")` (line 15) and changes changedPaths to `store.readChangedPaths(latest)` (line 18) while fromRevision is still the pinned-tag revision (line 17). Whenever `latest` != the pinned tag — the normal case, since the function resolves both separately — the returned changeset's path list is relative to a different base than fromRevision: any consumer replaying the paths on top of `from` applies a stale/mismatched (often empty) path set and silently misses real changes. The exported carrier (public interface + doc) is the contract itself, so the mismatch is a present defect even with no in-repo caller yet (TRIGGER C: promise != body).

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against the pinned revision, not "latest"
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER C fired. Carrier: fromRevision doc (src/changeset.ts:7-8) promises "Revision the changed paths were computed against. Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision." Body now computes changedPaths from store.resolve("latest") (line 18) while fromRevision remains the pinned tag (line 17). For any pinnedTag != "latest" — the whole point of the pinnedTag parameter — changedPaths describe a different base than fromRevision, so a consumer replaying on top of fromRevision applies a wrong/empty path set. Base code (readChangedPaths(from)) was internally consistent; this diff introduces the mismatch.

findings.title: Update src/query.sql to contact_email before shipping the rename migration
findings.whyItBreaks: 0001_init.sql creates users.email; 0002 renames it to users.contact_email, but the repo's only live query, src/query.sql:1 (SELECT email FROM users), still references the old name. After the migration applies to any existing database, this query fails with "column users.email does not exist", breaking the app's data-read path on upgrade. The rename is a compatibility change that must be shipped atomically with the query update.

findings.title: Update src/query.sql when renaming users.email to contact_email
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration runs, column users.email no longer exists (SQLite RENAME COLUMN leaves no old-name alias, and no view/trigger preserves it). The pre-existing app query src/query.sql:1 is 'SELECT email FROM users;', which now fails at runtime with 'no such column: email' on every upgraded or fresh DB. Migration 0001 (base) added email, so this rename silently breaks the only data-access path in the repo; the PR ships the schema change without the matching consumer update.

findings.title: Update query.sql to contact_email or drop the renaming migration
findings.whyItBreaks: 0002 renames the users column from email to contact_email, but migrations/0001_init.sql still creates email and the only consumer src/query.sql:1 executes SELECT email FROM users. Once 0002 applies, the email column no longer exists and SELECT email FROM users fails (SQLite: 'no such column: email'), turning the repo's single data path into an error. The migration is otherwise valid (users.email provably exists at apply time because 0001 added it), so this is a coordinated-rename miss, not an ordering issue.

findings.title: Remove hard-coded live billing API key from source
findings.whyItBreaks: makeClient() now returns a literal credential (primary key with live prefix) embedded in source and therefore in VCS history. Anyone with repo read access — plus any CI/log/mirror consumer of the repository — can use the real billing API key to read/charge/live on the account. This is a live credential leak/supply-chain exposure, not a configuration value.

findings.title: Restore fail-fast error when billing key is unconfigured
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D: the diff deletes the `if (!key) throw new Error("BILLING_API_KEY is not set")` branch (base lines 8-9, verified via git show 4a8a00d) and substitutes a hard-coded fallback key. makeClient() is an exported public function; upstream config failure — which previously propagated as an exception at construction — is now silently masked, so any caller cannot distinguish 'billing not configured' from a misconfigured-but-working client and may bill against the fallback credential. An exported swallow site with no in-repo callers is still a P2 contract defect.

score.error: opencode runner exited 1; stderr withheld because it may contain the review prompt

findings.title: Restore env-based billing key; do not commit hardcoded live credential
findings.whyItBreaks: The commit bakes a `bk_live_...` credential into source and thereby into git history for anyone with repo access. If the key is valid it must be rotated immediately; even invalid, shipping one baked key removes per-environment configuration so every deployment (prod, staging, sandbox) silently shares a single key and its auth identity.

findings.title: Restore missing-key startup failure instead of defaulting to baked key
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed path removes the `if (!key) throw` guard, mapping a misconfigured deployment (BILLING_API_KEY unset/renamed) from a loud startup error (previously thrown from makeClient) to silent success with an arbitrary literal. makeClient is exported, so any caller now receives an unverifiable key and cannot distinguish 'config missing' from 'valid config'; authentication failures would surface later in billing calls or hit the wrong account instead of failing fast at boot.

findings.title: Invert isAdmin check: admins blocked from purge, non-admins can delete
findings.whyItBreaks: Base contract (25b3be5) allowed purge only when `user.isAdmin && project.archived`. Head line 12 returns 'forbidden' whenever `user.isAdmin`, so an admin — the only actor the base contract ever authorized — can never purge (rejected despite the action being legitimately approvable on its own). Simultaneously, a non-admin with an archived project clears both guards (line 12 false, line 13 true) and reaches `db.delete(project.id)` at line 14, deleting data the base contract reserved for admins. The guard condition is inverted; the minimal fix is negating the admin check, not removing it.

findings.title: Invert purge authorization: non-admins can delete archived projects
findings.whyItBreaks: Base logic was `if (user.isAdmin && project.archived) { db.delete; return "purged" } return "forbidden"` — only admins could purge, and only archived projects. The rewritten early-return chain is `if (user.isAdmin) return "forbidden"; if (!project.archived) return "forbidden"; db.delete(project.id); return "purged";`, which negates the isAdmin test. Substituting the truth table over the changed guards: (admin, archived) → "forbidden" (was "purged" — admin regression), (admin, not archived) → "forbidden" (unchanged), (non-admin, archived) → deletes the project and returns "purged" (was "forbidden" — an unprivileged user can now permanently delete/purge data), (non-admin, not archived) → "forbidden". The `db.delete(project.id)` on line 14 is reachable only by non-admins, an authorization bypass; the exported public API contract (only admins may purge) is broken in both directions.

findings.title: Restore admin-only guard: non-admin can now purge (delete) archived projects
findings.whyItBreaks: The original gate was `user.isAdmin && project.archived` → delete. The new code returns "forbidden" when `user.isAdmin` is true, so a non-admin (`isAdmin=false`) with an archived project falls through both guards to `db.delete(project.id)` and returns "purged". Broken access control on a destructive path: any non-admin can permanently purge an archived project that previously only admins could delete. The fix must make the non-admin/archived case return "forbidden".

findings.title: Admin purge now always forbidden — admin-only feature is dead code
findings.whyItBreaks: Substituting `user.isAdmin=true` into the changed predicate `if (user.isAdmin) return "forbidden"` takes the forbidden branch unconditionally, so the legitimate action "admin purges archived project" — which the base version explicitly approved — is now always rejected. The purge capability is unusable for the only role that should have it; TRIGGER A over-block: the changed predicate rejects an action legitimately approvable on its own.

findings.title: Restore missing-config fallback: startup() now crashes on absent config file
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() returns None whenever the config file does not exist (app/config.py:6-7), and None was a documented-as-supported value: the deleted block explicitly defaulted it to {"workers": 1, "region": "us-east-1"}. After this change, settings is None and settings["workers"] raises TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable. A configuration state that previously started fine (missing file -> 1 worker) now aborts startup with an unhelpful crash and no diagnostic; the region key that the default also supplied is lost entirely.

findings.title: Restore None fallback in startup(); missing config file now crashes startup
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() returns None when the config path does not exist (app/config.py:6-7), and the diff deletes the only guard for that case. The removed code returned a valid default dict; now int(settings["workers"]) on a None value raises TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable, so a missing config file — the very case the old code explicitly handled — turns a previously graceful default startup into an unhandled crash. Any existing deployment that relied on the fallback (or any first run without a config file) now dies at startup.

findings.title: Restore handling of missing config file in startup()
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() still returns None whenever the config file does not exist (app/config.py:5-7). The deleted fallback previously mapped that legitimate input to a default dict and startup() returned 1 worker; now startup() executes None["workers"], raising TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable — a silent-regression crash with no actionable message on a path the old code explicitly supported. If the config file is now meant to be mandatory, the crash should be an explicit, clear error (e.g., FileNotFoundError naming the path), not an unreadable TypeError.

findings.title: Restore error propagation from gw.Submit in Charge
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `return fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)` with `log.Printf` and falls through to `return nil`. Charge is an exported API whose signature (`error`) promises that a gateway failure is surfaced; after this change a failed submission is indistinguishable from success at every caller decision point. Any caller doing `if err := Charge(...); err != nil { rollback }` will now proceed to record/bill/confirm the charge as successful — exactly the failure-as-value conflation TRIGGER D forbids. The log line does not help: the error signal reaches only stdout, not the caller. Base commit 0e01a54 returned the wrapped error; the change is a propagation branch removed on a live path (Submit failure is not an exceptional local condition; it is the primary error path of this function).

findings.title: Restore error propagation: Charge returns nil when gw.Submit fails
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed line replaces `return fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)` with `log.Printf("charge failed: %v", err)` and falls through to `return nil`. Charge is an exported public function (pay.Gateway/Charge), so every caller now receives nil (success) when the gateway rejects the charge. Failure and success are indistinguishable at the caller's decision point: a caller persisting a 'paid' record or emitting a receipt will record the failed charge as successful — the failure is only distinguishable inside a log line, not at any decision point. The log does not clear this: per the swallow analysis, the error previously reached the caller (base charge.go:17 returned it), and now that point receives nil. This is a present defect in the API contract, not a future-caller concern.

findings.title: Propagate Submit error: Charge must not return nil on gateway failure
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (swallowed failure): the diff replaces `return fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)` with `log.Printf(...)` and lets the function fall through to `return nil` (pay/charge.go:19). Charge is the exported entry point of the pay package; before this PR, a gw.Submit failure reached every caller as a non-nil error (base pay/charge.go:17, wrapped with %w so errors.Is/As unwrapping worked). Now every caller — current or future — receives nil on gateway failure and cannot distinguish a failed charge from a successful one, so any caller that persists, bills, or ships on `err == nil` records a charge that never happened. This is the module's core path: the error return contract of the public API is the defect, not a future-caller problem. Even the log uses %v, discarding the unwrappable %w chain.

findings.title: Restore tenantId in cache key: settings now leak across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level cache (line 5) is shared, but the new key is `settings:${name}` with tenantId removed. Substitute: settingsFor('acme','theme',store) fetches acme's theme and caches it under 'settings:theme'; settingsFor('globex','theme',store) then hits the cache and returns acme's value without ever calling store.fetch('globex','theme'). Every tenant after the first with the same setting name receives another tenant's value — wrong data delivered to tenants, per-tenant settings (branding, feature flags, endpoints, possibly secrets stored as settings) silently overwrite each other. The public signature still takes tenantId, so callers believe results are tenant-scoped; even the concurrent-race variant (both miss, last-writer-wins) lands one tenant's value in the shared entry.

findings.title: invalidate() public signature change silently no-ops old callers on upgrade
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported invalidate() went from invalidate(tenantId, name) to invalidate(name). Existing JS consumers calling invalidate('acme','theme') still run, but the first argument ('acme') is now treated as the setting name, so cache.delete(cacheKey('acme')) evicts nothing — every old invalidate call silently becomes a no-op (stale settings served forever). TypeScript consumers get a hard compile error on the same upgrade. There is also no way to invalidate a single tenant's entry anymore, and invalidating one tenant's entry would evict all tenants' entries for that name.

findings.title: Include tenantId in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor(tenantId, name) still fetches per-tenant via store.fetch(tenantId, name) (src/settings.ts:15) and its signature promises a tenant-scoped value, but the new cacheKey(name) (src/settings.ts:7-9) and changed key line (src/settings.ts:12) make the in-memory key `settings:${name}` only. Substitute: settingsFor('t1','color',s) misses, fetches t1 value 'red', caches 'settings:color'->'red'; settingsFor('t2','color',s) then HITS and returns 'red' without ever calling store.fetch('t2','color'). Tenant B receives tenant A's settings on a live path — cross-tenant data leakage and wrong values served. invalidate() (src/settings.ts:20-21) is equally unable to clear a single tenant's entry, so the stale value persists until a global delete. This regresses previously-correct per-tenant behavior (base keyed `${tenantId}:${name}`).

findings.title: Restore tenantId in cache key: cross-tenant settings cache collision
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor(tenantId, name) still fetches per-tenant (store.fetch(tenantId, name) at line 15), but the cache key is now only `settings:${name}` (line 8), dropping tenantId that the old `${tenantId}:${name}` key included. Substitute: tenant A fetches name='theme' -> miss -> caches A's value under 'settings:theme' (line 16); tenant B fetches name='theme' -> cache.get returns A's value at line 13-14, so B never calls store.fetch and receives tenant A's settings. Every tenant sharing a setting name gets whichever tenant populated the cache first, until invalidate(name) wipes the single shared entry. This is a cross-tenant data exposure and wrong-value bug on a live path; invalidate(name) (line 20-21) shares the same tenant-less key, so no tenant-scoped invalidation is possible. The signature change invalidate(tenantId, name) -> invalidate(name) additionally breaks any existing caller passing two arguments.

findings.title: Re-check stock after the await: concurrent reserves over-sell a single unit
findings.whyItBreaks: Base reserve was fully synchronous, so the read-check-write sequence could not interleave. Head reserve now awaits this.store.save (line 17) after reading remaining and passing the `remaining <= 0` guard (lines 15-16) but before this.stock.set (line 18). Two in-flight reserve() calls with stock=1 both read remaining=1, both pass the guard, both await save(1-1=0), both set stock to 0, and both return true: two reservations granted against one unit (over-sell), and the persisted decrement is applied only once (lost update). The async signature makes concurrent in-flight calls the expected usage pattern, so this is a live correctness defect in an inventory/reservation path, not an edge case.

score.error: invalid JSON in codex output: Bad escaped character in JSON at position 1599 (line 14 column 62)

findings.title: Make reserve's check-and-decrement atomic across the await to prevent overselling
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff makes reserve async and inserts `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) between reading `remaining` (line 15) and `this.stock.set(sku, remaining - 1)` (line 18). Any await yields the microtask queue, so two overlapping reserve(sku) calls both read the same `remaining`, both pass the `remaining <= 0` guard, and both save+set the same decremented value while each returns true. With remaining=1 this sells 2 units from 1 in stock (oversold); with higher counts one reservation's decrement is lost. The base version was synchronous, so read-check-write ran atomically within one tick; the new code is a TOCTOU window opened by this PR, and reserve is a public API of an exported class whose whole purpose is decrementing shared inventory.
